comments.content: @rndquu do you think this should be a separate repository's code, and as an integration with ubiquibot?
I'll work on breaking this down into detailed specifications later. But if somebody really wants to jumpstart this issue, I set a generous 1 week bounty time on it.

I'm still wondering if it makes sense to have a separate codebase because it's basically a full telegram bot that extends the UbiquiBot GitHub bot. 
Backend ideally should be a Cloudflare Worker. 
Just did a quick google search on implementations:
- https://github.com/codebam/cf-workers-telegram-bot
- https://github.com/cvzi/telegram-bot-cloudflare
This task requires that the bot should be able to be added to our group chat, and then create issues on GitHub based on messages that sound like a task is being delegated. 
- [ ] Setup bot
- [ ] Add bot to test group chat
- [ ] Intercept messages in test group chat with tagged users
- [ ] pass message to open ai api to gauge whether it thinks the message is delegating a task
- [ ] Create a new issue on GitHub with the message text, and a link to the message. Assign the tagged user handle (this assumes that their name matches on GitHub. If no match or failure then leave unassigned.) We can have a dedicated repo for these for now. 
- [ ] Post a reply in the telegram group chat with a link to the newly created issue
In the future we can associate telegram handles with GitHub usernames so we know who to assign to. 
We can also read the repository names and take a best guess of where the task should go based on the task contents, although that seems brittle.

I don't know but I would guess that PAT might make more sense because the bot needs to be added by a repository admin to their repos for access. No need to ask for access again for everyone via OAuth.

Resolves https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquibot/issues/424

In the first opening comment in your pull request to link it to any issue across any repository. Be sure to paste the entire URL to this issue.

Take the intercepted message and paste as the body of the GitHub issue, as a quoted text
And then copy the link of the Telegram message that was intercepted, and include it in the footer of the GitHub issue body. 
![image](https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquibot/assets/4975670/ddb89a35-ba45-41e1-9ab3-1063fc24f055)

This is only possible if: 
1. The Telegram username matches a GitHub username.
2. The GitHub user is added as a contributor to the repository.
Because of these requirements, I think that you should enable support for this. It is impossible to assign a GitHub user unless they are added to the repository. 
### A Future Case for Vector Databases: Contributor Recommendation
In the farther future I think its possible that we do implement the vector database because we want to parse every issue solved by every contributor (we could limit to the last 365 days) so that way, when a new issue is created, the bot can suggest specific contributors to work on it because the new issue is so similar to a previously solved issue by a contributor. 
That is intended to be across any repository that a contributor worked on. Even outside of our network of partners. 
I fear that the current approach might be too API call heavy for that use case, and that the vector database can serve as a cache while we slowly scrape all the contributor's last year of data after they register their wallet for the first time. 
Alternatively we could start monitoring from when they first sign up for the DevPool (ignore previously solved issues) so in this case: whenever a contributor solves a bounty, we could scrape the last interval of activity on their profile (e.g. the first day is the day that they registered their wallet for the first time) then we scrape between the time difference of the last scrape, and the closed bounty. This should make the scrape jobs across our network asynchronous, which should lighten the load on the infrastructure.)

Task checklist [here](https://github.com/ubiquity/ubiquibot/issues/424#issuecomment-1657074844). 
### Background 
Imagine if we made a chatgpt powered bot that monitors group chats (for example in our t.me/ubiquitydao) and when it thinks somebody is delegating a task (for example @jongropper can you reach out to the lawyer) it will post a message saying that a bounty was created and link to it right in the telegram. 
We can extend the concept to have chatgpt estimate how long the task should take. If it is confident with its time estimate (for example over 80%) then it can automatically set a time label. 
Finally the bounty will be manually approved by a project manager by setting the priority level. 
This will certainly at minimum help us stay organized on small task by recording them on GitHub. And at most we could have a very organic and seamless experience where tasks are being delegated (possibly even automatically assigned) and financially incentivized to happen soon. 
It could be a wonderfully efficient operating system. 
---
Ideally this should be configurable so that partners have fine-grained controls over how much to automate (how much they trust ChatGPT.)
- Set Priority
- Set Time
- Set Price
- Set Assignee
With maxed out permissions, the bot will create, fund, and manage tasks on the fly. However I feel that it doesn't seem like a good idea to max out the permissions at this stage. 
- We could have situations where we accidentally delegate too many initiatives to each contributor but eventually when we fine tune the system it might be!
  - more than 2 tasks is too many, but in this case it would be incredible to post them on a project board and the contributor can go down their task list in order
- The bot might have a difficult time estimating priority, but we could consider a `Priority: 0 (Normal)` default.

Could be very interesting to have some type of simple OAuth application that will post the issue on behalf of the user that sent the original message. This will allow them to be eligible for the comment incentives for creating a new issue.

I think a better approach will be to only listen to authorized Telegram handles' messages. Or a simpler implementation might be to check group permissions/if is admin?
Alternatively, it could operate slowly, keeping rate limits in mind?
This will also need configuration eventually! We will need a place in the database to keep the bot configs per channel.
